draft.title: Language and identity online
card: The way people speak and write shows who they are. It can also show which groups they belong to, such as a school, a team or a fan community.
Groups often share words, phrases and styles that outsiders may not know. Using them can signal that you are part of the group.
Online platforms create new words and ways of writing, such as abbreviations, memes, hashtags and emoji. People use them to signal identity.
A writer or speaker may change their language to suit the audience. A person might post differently in a gaming chat than in an email to a teacher.
draft.remember: Language choices can signal who we are and which group we belong to, online as well as face to face.

a.q: Why might a gaming community use its own slang in its chat?
opts: It signals that the speaker belongs to the group
It makes the messages longer and more formal
It shows the speaker is writing to a teacher
It stops anyone else from ever joining the chat
a.why: Shared slang can mark someone as part of a group, because members know it and outsiders may not. It does not stop others joining: it only signals who already belongs.
a.clue: Think about what shared words say about the people using them.

b.q: Priya writes relaxed posts full of slang and emoji on her fan forum. Her email to a museum is formal and has none. What does this show?
opts: She adapts her language to suit the audience
She has two different identities that are unrelated
She does not know how to write formally
Online language is always less correct than email
b.why: Priya changes her language for different audiences, and each style can signal a different side of who she is. Her forum posts do not show she cannot write formally, because she clearly can when the audience calls for it.
b.clue: She writes well in both places, but for different readers.

a.best: It signals that the speaker belongs to the group

b.best: She adapts her language to suit the audience

problems.detail: The why says shared slang 'only signals who already belongs', but the card says such words 'can signal' group membership. 'Only' overstates it, since shared slang can also exclude outsiders or build a sense of belonging.
